chapters.title: Chapter 1 - Establishment of European and British Rule in India
aliases: Establishment of European and British Rule in India

topics.title: Arrival of European Traders and Sea Routes
aliases: Establishment of European and British Rule in India
learning_objectives: Explain why European traders searched for sea routes to India after the fall of Constantinople in 1453 AD.
Trace the arrival of Portuguese (Vasco da Gama), Dutch, and French trading companies in India.
topics.explanation: When Constantinople fell to Turks in 1453 AD, overland trade routes connecting Europe to India were blocked. High demand for Indian spices (pepper, cardamom), cotton, and silk led European sailors to discover sea routes. Portuguese sailor Vasco da Gama reached Calicut in 1498 AD. Later, Dutch and French trading companies established factories along Indian coasts.
examples: Vasco da Gama landed at Calicut port on the Malabar coast in 1498 AD under King Zamorin's rule.
French East India Company established major trading centers at Pondicherry and Chandernagore.
exercises: Why did European nations search for a sea route to India in the 15th century?
Who was the first European sailor to reach India by sea and in which year?
solutions: The conquest of Constantinople by Turks in 1453 AD blocked land trade routes, making new sea routes necessary to obtain Indian spices, cotton, and silk.
Vasco da Gama of Portugal reached Calicut in 1498 AD.
practice_questions: Name two items in high demand in Europe exported from India.
Which European power established its headquarters at Goa?

topics.title: English East India Company and Anglo-French Rivalry
learning_objectives: Describe the establishment of the English East India Company under Queen Elizabeth's charter in 1600 AD.
Explain Anglo-French rivalries (Carnatic Wars) resulting in British trading dominance.
topics.explanation: Queen Elizabeth I granted a charter to English East India Company in 1600 AD for trade monopoly with the East. Captain Hawkins and Sir Thomas Roe obtained trade permissions (farmans) from Mughal Emperor Jahangir to build factories in Surat and Madras. Rivalry between English and French companies led to three Carnatic Wars, ending in British supremacy.
examples: Sir Thomas Roe obtained permission from Jahangir in 1615 AD to establish British factories in Mughal territory.
British victory in the Carnatic Wars eliminated French political power in India.
exercises: Which Mughal Emperor granted permission to the British East India Company to set up a factory at Surat?
What was the main outcome of Anglo-French rivalries in South India?
solutions: Emperor Jahangir.
The English East India Company defeated the French, securing a political and commercial monopoly in India.
practice_questions: In which year was the English East India Company formed?
What was Fort William?
practice_solutions: The fortified settlement built by the British East India Company in Calcutta (Kolkata).

topics.title: Battle of Plassey (1757) and Battle of Buxar (1764)
aliases: Battle of Plassey Sirajuddaulah Mir Jafar
learning_objectives: Analyze causes and consequences of Battle of Plassey (1757) and Battle of Buxar (1764).
Explain how the Company acquired Diwani (tax collection) rights over Bengal, Bihar, and Orissa.
topics.explanation: In 1757, Robert Clive defeated Nawab Siraj-ud-Daulah of Bengal at Plassey due to treachery by commander Mir Jafar. In 1764, British defeated combined forces of Mir Qasim, Shuja-ud-Daulah, and Shah Alam II at Buxar. Treaty of Allahabad (1765) granted Company legal Diwani rights to collect land revenues in Bengal, Bihar, and Orissa.
examples: Battle of Plassey transformed the British East India Company from traders into political masters of Bengal.
Diwani rights gave the British control over Bengal's vast treasury, financing their trade and military expansion.
exercises: Explain the significance of the Battle of Plassey (1757) in Indian history.
What political privilege did the Treaty of Allahabad (1765) grant to the British East India Company?
solutions: It marked the beginning of British territorial rule in India as the Company gained control over Bengal.
Diwani rights, allowing the British to collect revenue directly from Bengal, Bihar, and Orissa.
practice_questions: Who led the British forces in the Battle of Plassey?
Which three rulers fought against the British in the Battle of Buxar (1764)?
practice_solutions: Mir Qasim (Bengal), Shuja-ud-Daulah (Awadh), and Shah Alam II (Mughal Emperor).

chapters.title: Chapter 2 - British Rule in India (1757 AD to 1857 AD)
aliases: British Rule in India (1757 AD to 1857 AD)

topics.title: Revenue Systems: Permanent Settlement, Ryotwari and Mahalwari
aliases: British Rule in India (1757 AD to 1857 AD)
learning_objectives: Compare the three British land revenue systems: Permanent Settlement (1793), Ryotwari (1820), and Mahalwari (1822).
Evaluate their oppressive impact on Indian farmers.
topics.explanation:
To maximize revenues, British introduced three land revenue systems:
- Permanent Settlement (Cornwallis, 1793, Bengal): Fixed revenue permanently with landlords (Zamindars).
- Ryotwari System (Munro, 1820, Madras/Bombay): Revenue fixed directly with individual cultivators (Ryots).
- Mahalwari System (Mackenzie, 1822, NW Provinces): Revenue collected collectively from village communities (Mahal).
examples: Under Permanent Settlement, peasants lost land ownership if Zamindars failed to pay fixed revenue by sunset date.
Ryotwari system subjected cultivators to high direct tax demands, driving farmers into debt traps.
exercises: Who introduced Permanent Settlement in Bengal and in which year?
Differentiate between Permanent Settlement and Ryotwari system.
solutions: Lord Cornwallis in 1793 AD.
Permanent Settlement fixed tax permanently with Zamindars (landlords), whereas Ryotwari settled tax directly with Ryots (cultivators) periodically.
practice_questions: What does the term 'Mahal' mean in the Mahalwari system?
Why were Indian farmers impoverished under British land revenue systems?
practice_solutions: A village or group of villages.
Exorbitant tax rates, rigid collection even during droughts, and exploitation by moneylenders.

topics.title: Impact on Indian Peasantry and Commercialisation of Crops
aliases: forced cash crops opium indigo tea
learning_objectives: Explain commercialisation of agriculture forcing farmers to grow cash crops (Indigo, Opium, Cotton).
Describe the Indigo Revolt (Nij and Ryoti cultivation systems).
topics.explanation: British forced Indian farmers to grow commercial cash crops (indigo, opium, tea, cotton) for British industries instead of food grains. Indigo planters coerced farmers under oppressive advance loan contracts (Ryoti system). Severe exploitation triggered the Indigo Revolt of 1859 in Bengal.
examples: Planters forced farmers to cultivate indigo on their most fertile land, ruining soil fertility for rice crops.
Deenabandhu Mitra wrote the play 'Nil Darpan' highlighting the plight of indigo cultivators.
exercises: What was the Indigo Revolt of 1859?
How did commercialisation of agriculture affect food security in India?
solutions: A widespread peasant uprising in Bengal against European planters forcing farmers to grow indigo on oppressive terms.
Shifting land from food grains (rice/wheat) to cash crops caused artificial food shortages and severe famines.
practice_questions: Name the play written by Deenabandhu Mitra on indigo planters.
What were the two main systems of indigo cultivation?
practice_solutions: Nij cultivation (on planter's own land) and Ryoti cultivation (on farmer's land under contract).

topics.title: Economic Drain Theory and De-industrialisation
learning_objectives: Explain Dadabhai Naoroji's Economic Drain Theory (Poverty and Un-British Rule in India).
Analyze de-industrialisation: collapse of Indian handicrafts and weaver livelihoods.
topics.explanation: Dadabhai Naoroji formulated the 'Drain of Wealth' theory, explaining how wealth (salaries, pensions, profits, home charges) was continuously siphoned from India to Britain without economic return. One-way free trade flooded Indian markets with cheap Manchester machine-made cloth, destroying traditional Indian weaver communities.
examples: Machine-made cloth imported from England destroyed famous handloom textile centers like Dacca (Dhaka).
Dadabhai Naoroji published his findings in 'Poverty and Un-British Rule in India'.
exercises: Who propounded the 'Drain of Wealth' theory?
What was the primary cause of de-industrialisation of Indian handicrafts in the 19th century?
solutions: Dadabhai Naoroji.
Inflow of cheap machine-made British goods combined with high protective tariffs imposed on Indian export goods in Britain.
practice_questions: Name Dadabhai Naoroji's famous book on Indian economy.
Why did traditional weavers lose their livelihoods under British rule?
practice_solutions: Poverty and Un-British Rule in India.
They could not compete with cheap machine-made cloth imported tariff-free from Manchester factories.

chapters.title: Chapter 3 - India's First War of Independence

topics.title: Causes of the 1857 Revolt
learning_objectives: Examine political, economic, socio-religious, and military causes of the 1857 Revolt.
Identify the immediate cause: introduction of greased Enfield rifle cartridges.
topics.explanation:
Causes of 1857 War:
- Political: Lord Dalhousie's Doctrine of Lapse (annexing Satara, Jhansi, Nagpur) and Awadh annexation.
- Economic: Ruin of artisans and high land taxes.
- Social/Religious: Interference in customs and fear of forced conversions.
- Military: Pay discrimination against Indian Sepoys.
- Immediate Cause: Greased cartridges for Enfield rifles allegedly coated with cow/pig fat, offending Hindu and Muslim sepoys.
examples: Dalhousie annexed Jhansi using Doctrine of Lapse when Rani Laxmibai's adopted son was denied royal succession.
Sepoy Mangal Pandey refused Enfield cartridges at Barrackpore in March 1857.
exercises: What was Lord Dalhousie's Policy of Annexation called?
What was the immediate cause of the 1857 Revolt?
solutions: Doctrine of Lapse.
Introduction of Enfield rifle cartridges greased with cow and pig fat, which offended religious sentiments of Hindu and Muslim soldiers.
practice_questions: Which soldier fired the first shot of the 1857 revolt at Barrackpore?
Name two princely states annexed under the Doctrine of Lapse.
topics.marks_pattern: State the key social-science idea, support it with relevant evidence or an example, and connect it directly to the question.

topics.title: Main Centres and Key Leaders of the Revolt
aliases: Tatya Tope Nana Saheb Kunwar Singh
learning_objectives: Identify major centers (Delhi, Kanpur, Lucknow, Jhansi, Bihar, Gujarat) and prominent leaders of the 1857 Revolt.
Describe contributions of Rani Laxmibai, Nana Saheb, Tatya Tope, and Kunwar Singh.
topics.explanation:
The 1857 uprising spread across Northern and Central India:
- Delhi: Bahadur Shah Zafar declared Emperor of India.
- Kanpur: Nana Saheb and General Tatya Tope.
- Jhansi: Rani Laxmibai valiantly fought British troops.
- Lucknow: Begum Hazrat Mahal.
- Bihar: 80-year-old landlord Kunwar Singh.
- Gujarat: Uprising in Anand (Garbad Das Patel), Patan, and Dwarka.
examples: Rani Laxmibai of Jhansi died fighting bravely on the battlefield at Gwalior.
Garbad Das Patel led local freedom fighters in Anand, Gujarat against British forces.
exercises: Name the prominent leaders who led the 1857 uprising in Kanpur and Jhansi.
Who was declared the nominal leader/emperor of India by revolting sepoys in Delhi?
solutions: Kanpur: Nana Saheb and Tatya Tope; Jhansi: Rani Laxmibai.
Mughal Emperor Bahadur Shah Zafar II.
practice_questions: Which 80-year-old leader led the revolt in Jagdishpur, Bihar?
Mention the role of Garbad Das Patel in Gujarat during 1857.
practice_solutions: He mobilized local mukhis and farmers in Anand region against British rule.

topics.title: Failure of the Revolt and End of Company Rule
learning_objectives: Analyze reasons for failure of the 1857 Revolt (lack of central leadership, localized outbreak, modern British weaponry).
Explain Queen Victoria's Proclamation of 1858 ending East India Company rule and establishing British Crown Rule.
topics.explanation: Reasons for Failure: Lack of unified central command, superior British weapons/telegraph/railways, and lack of support from certain princely states. Outcome: Government of India Act 1858 abolished East India Company rule. Power transferred directly to British Crown under Queen Victoria's Proclamation, represented by a Viceroy.
examples: Queen Victoria's Proclamation promised non-interference in religious matters and equal legal treatment.
The title of Governor-General was changed to Viceroy of India starting with Lord Canning in 1858.
exercises: State two major causes for the failure of the 1857 Revolt.
What major constitutional change took place in India under the Government of India Act 1858?
solutions: Lack of central leadership/coordination and superior military organization/weapons of the British.
Rule of East India Company ended and direct rule of the British Crown was established in India.
practice_questions: Who became the first Viceroy of India in 1858?
What promise did Queen Victoria make regarding Indian princely territories?
practice_solutions: To respect treaty rights and abandon further territorial annexation.

chapters.title: Chapter 4 - Cities, Cottage Industries and Industries of the British Period
aliases: Cities, Cottage Industries and Industries of the British Period

topics.title: De-urbanization of Old Cities and Rise of Colonial Ports
aliases: Cities, Cottage Industries and Industries of the British Period
learning_objectives: Explain de-urbanization of traditional Indian court cities (Surat, Murshidabad, Dacca).
Describe growth of new British Presidency port cities (Bombay, Calcutta, Madras).
topics.explanation: As regional royal courts collapsed and trade shifted, traditional trading cities like Surat, Masulipatnam, and Murshidabad declined (de-urbanization). Meanwhile, British established new Presidency urban centers around major ports: Bombay (Mumbai), Calcutta (Kolkata), and Madras (Chennai).
examples: Surat lost its status as India's premier western trade port when British developed Bombay port.
Calcutta grew rapidly as the administrative capital of British India until 1911.
exercises: What is de-urbanization?
Name the three British Presidency port cities that expanded during the colonial period.
solutions: The decline and depopulation of traditional historic cities due to economic decay or loss of political court status.
Bombay (Mumbai), Calcutta (Kolkata), and Madras (Chennai).
practice_questions: Which major western port city declined as Bombay developed?
When was the capital of British India shifted from Calcutta to Delhi?

topics.title: Decline of Indian Cottage Industries and Handloom Textiles
learning_objectives: Analyze causes for ruin of Indian handlooms, spinning wheels (charkha), and cottage handicrafts.
Describe impact of British free-trade policy on Indian artisan households.
topics.explanation: Before British rule, Indian textiles (Dacca Muslin, Calico, Chintz) dominated world trade. British Industrial Revolution produced cheap factory cloth. British imposed heavy import duties on Indian goods entering Britain while importing British factory cloth tariff-free into India, ruining millions of cottage weavers.
examples: World-famous Dacca Muslin fine cotton fabric lost global markets due to British trade tariffs.
Millions of rural weavers lost employment and turned into landless agricultural labourers.
exercises: Why did traditional Indian handloom weavers lose their livelihood during the British period?
What was Dacca famous for in textile history?
solutions: They could not compete with cheap machine-made cloth imported from Britain and faced heavy export taxes in Europe.
Extremely fine quality cotton fabric known as Dacca Muslin.
practice_questions: What was 'Calico'?
How did ruin of cottage industries affect rural agriculture?
practice_solutions: Indian cotton cloth named after Calicut port where Portuguese first traded it.
Unemployed artisans migrated to villages, overcrowding agricultural land as daily-wage laborers.

topics.title: Rise of Modern Industries: Steel and Textiles in India
learning_objectives: Trace establishment of modern cotton textile mills (Mumbai 1854, Ahmedabad 1861).
Describe growth of iron and steel industry: TISCO established by Jamsetji Tata at Jamshedpur (1907).
topics.explanation: First modern cotton textile mill was established in Mumbai (1854). Ranchhodlal Chhotalal started Ahmedabad's first cotton mill in 1861, earning Ahmedabad the title 'Manchester of India'. Jamsetji Tata established Tata Iron and Steel Company (TISCO) at Sakchi (Jamshedpur) in 1907, pioneering Indian heavy industry.
examples: Ahmedabad became a leading cotton textile hub due to proximity to black cotton soil of Gujarat.
TISCO Jamshedpur supplied steel rails for Indian Railways during World War I.
exercises: Who founded Tata Iron and Steel Company (TISCO) and in which year?
Why was Ahmedabad called the 'Manchester of India'?
solutions: Jamsetji Tata in 1907 AD (at Sakchi, Jamshedpur).
Because of its rapid growth as a major cotton textile manufacturing center like Manchester in England.
practice_questions: Who established the first cotton mill in Ahmedabad in 1861?
In which city was India's first successful cotton textile mill set up in 1854?

chapters.title: Chapter 5 - Education and Social System During the British Rule
aliases: Education and Social System During the British Rule

topics.title: Orientalist vs Anglicist Controversy and Wood's Despatch (1854)
aliases: Education and Social System During the British Rule
learning_objectives: Differentiate between Orientalists (promoting Sanskrit/Persian) and Anglicists (promoting English education).
Explain Macaulay's Minute (1835) and Wood's Despatch (1854) as foundation of modern western education.
topics.explanation: British debate on education pitted Orientalists (William Jones, advocating Sanskrit and Persian learning) against Anglicists (Lord Macaulay, advocating English education). Macaulay's Minute (1835) made English the official medium. Charles Wood's Despatch (1854) introduced a comprehensive education system (primary, secondary, university) called Magna Carta of English Education in India.
examples: Wood's Despatch of 1854 led to creation of Education Departments in all provinces.
Universities of Calcutta, Bombay, and Madras were established in 1857 following Wood's Despatch.
exercises: What was Lord Macaulay's recommendation regarding the medium of instruction in India in 1835?
Why is Wood's Despatch (1854) called the Magna Carta of modern Indian education?
solutions: He recommended English as the official medium of higher instruction in place of Persian and Sanskrit.
Because it laid a systematic framework for primary, secondary, and university education across India.
practice_questions: Name three universities established in India in 1857.
Who founded the Asiatic Society of Bengal to study oriental literature?
practice_solutions: Universities of Calcutta, Bombay, and Madras.

topics.title: Growth of Vernacular Education and National Institutions
learning_objectives: Evaluate William Adam's report on indigenous village pathshalas.
Describe national education initiatives: Rabindranath Tagore's Shantiniketan and Mahatma Gandhi's Gujarat Vidyapith (1920).
topics.explanation:
William Adam surveyed 100,000 village pathshalas in Bengal and Bihar with flexible timetables. Later, national leaders opposed purely western colonial education and founded indigenous institutions:
- Rabindranath Tagore established Visva-Bharati Shantiniketan (1901) combining nature and arts.
- Mahatma Gandhi founded Gujarat Vidyapith (Ahmedabad, 1920) during Non-Cooperation Movement for self-reliant education.
examples: Shantiniketan held classes in open air under trees to foster natural learning.
Gujarat Vernacular Society (established 1848 by Alexander Forbes and Kavi Dalpatram) promoted Gujarati language literature.
exercises: Who established Visva-Bharati at Shantiniketan?
Why did Mahatma Gandhi found Gujarat Vidyapith at Ahmedabad in 1920?
solutions: Rabindranath Tagore.
To provide national self-reliant education in mother tongue outside British government control during Non-Cooperation Movement.
practice_questions: Name the British officer who prepared a report on indigenous pathshalas in Bengal.
Who founded the Gujarat Vernacular Society in 1848?
practice_solutions: Alexander Kinloch Forbes (supported by poet Dalpatram).

topics.title: Social Reform Movements: Sati Abolition, Widow Remarriage and Caste Reform
aliases: Raja Ram Mohan Roy Brahmo Samaj Sati 1829
learning_objectives: Identify social reformers and their achievements: Raja Ram Mohan Roy (Brahmo Samaj, Sati Prohibition Act 1829), Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar (Widow Remarriage Act 1856).
Describe caste and women empowerment reforms (Dayanand Saraswati, Jyotirao Phule, Swami Vivekananda).
topics.explanation:
Indian Renaissance reform movements:
- Raja Ram Mohan Roy (Brahmo Samaj): Persuaded Lord William Bentinck to pass Sati Prohibition Act (1829).
- Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar: Helped pass Hindu Widow Remarriage Act (1856).
- Swami Dayanand Saraswati (Arya Samaj): Slogan 'Go back to the Vedas' and opposed caste discrimination.
- Jyotirao Phule (Satyashodhak Samaj): Fought for lower-caste education and women's rights.
examples: Brahmo Samaj campaigned against female infanticide, child marriage, and Sati system.
Jyotirao Phule and his wife Savitribai Phule opened India's first girls' school in Pune in 1848.
exercises: Who helped Lord William Bentinck enact the law banning Sati practice in 1829?
Which social reformer was instrumental in passing the Hindu Widow Remarriage Act of 1856?
solutions: Raja Ram Mohan Roy.
Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar.
practice_questions: Who founded Arya Samaj and gave the call 'Go back to Vedas'?
Name the organization founded by Jyotirao Phule for social equality.

chapters.title: Chapter 6 - Freedom Movements (1885 AD to 1947 AD)

topics.title: Formation of INC (1885), Moderates and Extremists
learning_objectives: Explain formation of Indian National Congress (1885) under A.O. Hume and W.C. Bonnerjee.
Differentiate between Moderate leaders (Dadabhai Naoroji, Gokhale) and Extremist leaders (Lal-Bal-Pal: Tilak, Lajpat Rai, Bipin Chandra Pal).
topics.explanation: Indian National Congress was founded in December 1885 at Bombay by A.O. Hume; first President was W.C. Bonnerjee. Early leaders were Moderates who used petitions and constitutional methods. By 1905, Extremist leaders led by 'Lal-Bal-Pal' demanded Swaraj (Self-rule). Lokmanya Tilak declared: 'Swaraj is my birthright and I shall have it!'
examples: The first session of Indian National Congress was attended by 72 delegates at Gokuldas Tejpal Sanskrit College in Bombay.
Bal Gangadhar Tilak started newspapers 'Kesari' (Marathi) and 'Mahratta' (English) to awaken national consciousness.
exercises: When and where was the Indian National Congress founded?
Who gave the famous slogan 'Swaraj is my birthright and I shall have it!'?
solutions: In December 1885 at Gokuldas Tejpal Sanskrit College in Bombay.
Lokmanya Bal Gangadhar Tilak.
practice_questions: Name two Moderate leaders of early INC.
Who was the first President of the Indian National Congress?
practice_solutions: Dadabhai Naoroji and Gopal Krishna Gokhale.

topics.title: Partition of Bengal, Swadeshi, Non-Cooperation and Dandi March
learning_objectives: Examine Partition of Bengal (1905) by Lord Curzon leading to Swadeshi & Boycott Movement.
Describe Gandhi's Non-Cooperation Movement (1920) and Civil Disobedience Movement (Dandi March, 1930).
topics.explanation: Lord Curzon partitioned Bengal in 1905 to divide Hindus and Muslims, provoking Banga-Bhanga agitation and Swadeshi Movement (boycotting foreign goods). Mahatma Gandhi launched Non-Cooperation Movement in 1920. In March 1930, Gandhi marched from Sabarmati Ashram to Dandi coast (385 km) to break the unjust Salt Law.
examples: On 6th April 1930, Gandhi picked up a handful of salt at Dandi, breaking British Salt Law monopoly.
People burnt foreign cloth bonfires during Swadeshi and Non-Cooperation movements.
exercises: Why did Lord Curzon partition Bengal in 1905?
Explain the significance of the Dandi March (1930) led by Mahatma Gandhi.
solutions: To weaken Indian national unity under the pretext of administrative efficiency by creating religious division.
It launched the Civil Disobedience Movement as Gandhi marched to Dandi and broke the oppressive British Salt Monopoly.
practice_questions: From where did Mahatma Gandhi start the historic Dandi March?
Why did Gandhi withdraw the Non-Cooperation Movement in 1922?
practice_solutions: Due to the violent Chauri Chaura incident in Uttar Pradesh where a police station was set on fire.

topics.title: Quit India Movement (1942), INA and Independence (1947)
aliases: Quit India Movement Do or Die 1942
Subhash Chandra Bose Azad Hind Fauj INA
learning_objectives: Explain Quit India Movement (1942) and Gandhi's slogan 'Do or Die'.
Describe Netaji Subhash Chandra Bose, Azad Hind Fauj (INA), and Mountbatten Plan leading to Indian Independence on 15 August 1947.
topics.explanation: In August 1942, Congress passed Quit India resolution in Mumbai; Gandhi gave slogan 'Do or Die'. Netaji Subhash Chandra Bose formed Azad Hind Fauj (INA) in Singapore with slogans 'Jai Hind' and 'Chalo Delhi!'. Under Mountbatten Plan, British India was partitioned into India and Pakistan, gaining independence on 15 August 1947.
examples: Netaji Subhash Chandra Bose established the Provisional Government of Free India in Singapore.
India achieved freedom at midnight on 15 August 1947, with Jawaharlal Nehru as first Prime Minister.
exercises: What call did Mahatma Gandhi give to the nation during the Quit India Movement of 1942?
Who led the Azad Hind Fauj (Indian National Army) with the slogan 'Chalo Delhi'?
solutions: 'Do or Die' (Karo ya Maro).
Netaji Subhash Chandra Bose.

Who was India's first Prime Minister?

topics.title: Modern Indian Painting and Bengal School of Art
aliases: Abanindranath Tagore Bengal School Bharat Mata
learning_objectives: Trace evolution of modern Indian painting: Raja Ravi Varma (realism, oil painting of epics).
Describe Bengal School of Art established by Abanindranath Tagore (swadeshi art, 'Bharat Mata' painting).
topics.explanation:
Modern Indian painting developed distinct schools:
- Raja Ravi Varma (Kerala) blended Western oil technique with Indian mythological themes (Shakuntala, Nala-Damayanti).
- Bengal School led by Abanindranath Tagore and Nandalal Bose rejected Western realism, drawing inspiration from Ajanta caves and Indian heritage. Abanindranath painted the famous 'Bharat Mata'.
examples: Raja Ravi Varma set up a printing press in Mumbai to make lithograph prints of Indian gods affordable for common people.
Abanindranath Tagore depicted Bharat Mata as an ascetic woman offering food, cloth, learning, and spiritual peace.
exercises: Why is Raja Ravi Varma considered a pioneer of modern Indian painting?
Who painted the iconic image of 'Bharat Mata' during the Bengal School movement?
solutions: He successfully combined Western oil technique with Indian mythological and epic themes, making art accessible to all.
Abanindranath Tagore.
practice_questions: Which ancient cave paintings inspired the Bengal School of Art?
Where did Raja Ravi Varma establish his lithographic printing press?

topics.title: Colonial Architecture and Urban Monuments
learning_objectives: Identify colonial architectural styles (Gothic revival, Indo-Saracenic, Neoclassical).
Describe iconic structures: Victoria Terminus (CST Mumbai), Gateway of India, and Lutyens' New Delhi (Rashtrapati Bhavan, Parliament House).
topics.explanation:
British constructed grand public buildings blending European and Indian elements (Indo-Saracenic architecture):
- Gothic Revival: Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj Terminus (Victoria Terminus) in Mumbai.
- Indo-Saracenic: Gateway of India in Mumbai (1911) designed by George Wittet.
- Delhi Capital Architecture: Designed by Edwin Lutyens and Herbert Baker (Viceroy's House/Rashtrapati Bhavan, Parliament House).
examples: Gateway of India was built to commemorate the visit of King George V and Queen Mary in 1911.

topics.explanation:

examples: NDRF teams deploy boats and helicopters to rescue stranded citizens during heavy monsoon floods in Gujarat.
Applying cold running water immediately on minor burns reduces tissue damage before medical help arrives.
exercises: What is NDRF and what is its role during natural disasters?
State two duties of responsible citizens during a disaster.
solutions: National Disaster Response Force; a specialized force trained for rapid rescue, evacuation, and relief operations.
Avoid spreading unverified rumors and help vulnerable neighbors (elderly/children) move to safe shelters.
practice_questions: What emergency helpline number can be dialed for disaster relief in India?
What is the first step in administering first aid for minor thermal burns?
practice_solutions: Cool the burn with clean running tap water for at least 10 minutes.

topics.title: Need for a Constitution and Framing of Indian Constitution

learning_objectives: Explain why a democratic nation needs a Constitution.
Describe the Constituent Assembly (Dr. Rajendra Prasad President, Dr. B.R. Ambedkar Drafting Committee Chairman) and enactment on 26 January 1950.
topics.explanation: A Constitution is a fundamental document of supreme law governing a country. Constituent Assembly started work on 9 Dec 1946 with Dr. Rajendra Prasad as President and Dr. B.R. examples: Dr. B.R. Ambedkar is revered as the 'Father of the Indian Constitution' for guiding its drafting.
26th January was chosen for Republic Day to honor the 1930 Poorna Swaraj declaration.
exercises: Who was the Chairman of the Drafting Committee of the Indian Constitution?
On which date did the Constitution of India come into force?
solutions: Dr. Bhimrao Ramji Ambedkar.
26th January 1950.

How long did the Constituent Assembly take to draft the Indian Constitution?

topics.title: Key Features: Preamble, Secularism, Federalism and Parliamentary System
aliases: Preamble sovereign socialist secular democratic republic
learning_objectives: Analyze Preamble values: Sovereign, Socialist, Secular, Democratic, Republic.
Explain core constitutional pillars: Federalism, Separation of Powers, and Universal Adult Franchise (18+ years voting right).
topics.explanation:
Core Pillars:
- Preamble: Introduction stating goals of Justice, Liberty, Equality, Fraternity.
- Secularism: State treats all religions equally without adopting any official state religion.
- Federalism: Power divided between Central Government and State Governments.
- Universal Adult Franchise: Every Indian citizen aged 18 or above has equal right to vote regardless of caste, gender, or wealth.
examples: In India, a citizen aged 18 can vote in elections regardless of income or background.
Federal system grants State Governments jurisdiction over police and public health while Union Government handles defense and foreign affairs.
exercises: What is meant by a 'Secular State' in the Indian Constitution?
What is Universal Adult Franchise?
solutions: A state that does not have any official state religion and treats all religious communities with equal respect and freedom.
The constitutional right of every citizen who has attained 18 years of age to vote in elections without discrimination.
practice_questions: What is Federalism?
List four key values declared in the Preamble to the Indian Constitution.
practice_solutions: A system of government where political power is divided between a central national government and state governments.

topics.title: Fundamental Rights and Fundamental Duties
aliases: Right to Equality Freedom Constitutional Remedies
learning_objectives: Identify Six Fundamental Rights guaranteed under Part III (Articles 14 to 32).
Explain Fundamental Duties (Article 51A) promoting civic responsibility and peaceful constitutional observance.
topics.explanation:
Part III guarantees Six Fundamental Rights:
1) Right to Equality
2) Right to Freedom
3) Right against Exploitation
4) Right to Freedom of Religion
5) Cultural & Educational Rights
6) Right to Constitutional Remedies (Dr. Ambedkar called it the 'Heart and Soul of the Constitution').
Article 51A outlines Fundamental Duties (respecting national flag, protecting environment, preserving heritage).
examples: Right to Constitutional Remedies allows any citizen to approach High Court or Supreme Court if their rights are violated.
Abiding by the Constitution, honoring the National Flag, and safeguarding public property are Fundamental Duties.
exercises: Why did Dr. B.R. Ambedkar call the Right to Constitutional Remedies the 'Heart and Soul' of the Constitution?
State two Fundamental Duties of Indian citizens under Article 51A.
solutions: Because it allows citizens to directly move the High Court or Supreme Court to enforce their Fundamental Rights if infringed.
To respect the National Flag and National Anthem, and to protect the natural environment (forests, rivers, wildlife).
practice_questions: How many Fundamental Rights are guaranteed by Part III of the Indian Constitution?
Which article of the Constitution lays down Fundamental Duties?

topics.title: Structure and Role of the Indian Parliament
aliases: Lok Sabha House of People 543 members
Rajya Sabha Council of States 245 members
learning_objectives: Describe bicameral structure of Indian Parliament: Lok Sabha (House of the People, 543 elected) and Rajya Sabha (Council of States, 245 members).
Explain role of President as part of Parliament.
topics.explanation:
Parliament (Sansad) is the supreme law-making organ of Indian democracy consisting of President, Lok Sabha, and Rajya Sabha:
- Lok Sabha: Lower House, 543 members directly elected by people for a 5-year term. Speaker presides.
- Rajya Sabha: Upper House, 245 members (233 elected by state assemblies + 12 nominated by President). Vice President is ex-officio Chairman.
examples: Voters in parliamentary constituencies elect Members of Parliament (MPs) to represent them in Lok Sabha.
Rajya Sabha is a permanent house that is never dissolved; one-third members retire every two years.
exercises: Name the two Houses of the Indian Parliament.
What is the term of Lok Sabha and who presides over its proceedings?
solutions: Lok Sabha (House of the People) and Rajya Sabha (Council of States).
5 years; the Speaker presides over Lok Sabha proceedings.
practice_questions: Who is the ex-officio Chairman of Rajya Sabha?
How many members are nominated by the President to Rajya Sabha?
practice_solutions: 12 members (distinguished in literature, science, art, and social service).

topics.title: How Laws are Made in Parliament
learning_objectives: Trace the step-by-step legislative process of converting a Bill into an Act of Law.
Differentiate between Ordinary Bills and Money Bills.
topics.explanation:
Lawmaking Process:
1) Introduction & First Reading: Bill presented in either house.
2) Second Reading: Clause-by-clause discussion and committee review.
3) Third Reading: Voting on final text.
4) Other House Approval: Sent to second house for passage.
5) Presidential Assent: Bill becomes an Act (Law) when President signs it. Money Bills can only be introduced in Lok Sabha.
examples: RTI (Right to Information) Bill was passed by both houses of Parliament and became law after receiving Presidential assent in 2005.
Money Bills require prior recommendation of the President and can originate only in Lok Sabha.
exercises: When does a proposed Bill officially become a Law in India?
In which House of Parliament can a Money Bill be introduced?
solutions: When it is passed by both Houses of Parliament and receives the formal assent of the President of India.
Only in the Lok Sabha.
practice_questions: What happens during the Second Reading of a Bill in Parliament?
Who decides whether a Bill is a Money Bill or an Ordinary Bill?
practice_solutions: Detailed clause-by-clause debate, amendments, and examination by parliamentary committees.
The Speaker of the Lok Sabha.

topics.title: Rule of Law, Unpopular Laws and Peaceful Democratic Protests
learning_objectives: Explain Rule of Law (all citizens equal before law; no one above law).
Describe peaceful democratic methods (rallies, petitions, media debate) to oppose unpopular laws (Civic Safety: peaceful participation only).
topics.explanation: Rule of Law means law applies equally to all citizens regardless of position, wealth, or power. If Parliament passes an unpopular or unjust law that conflicts with public interest or Constitution, citizens have the right to express peaceful dissent through public meetings, media debate, peaceful marches, and court petitions (Judicial Review). Protests MUST remain peaceful and non-violent without damaging public property.
examples: Citizens filing petitions in Supreme Court to challenge an unconstitutional law.
Holding peaceful public meetings and submitting memoranda to elected representatives.
exercises: What does 'Rule of Law' signify in a democracy?
Civic Safety: How should citizens express opposition to an unpopular law in a democracy?
solutions: That all individuals are equal before the law, and no person—regardless of rank or wealth—is above the law.
Through peaceful, lawful democratic methods such as filing court petitions, peaceful rallies, media discussions, and writing to representatives without violence or property damage.
practice_questions: What power allows the Supreme Court to strike down an unconstitutional law passed by Parliament?
Why is peaceful non-violent protest essential in democratic civic life?
practice_solutions: It allows citizens to voice genuine grievances and influence policy while upholding law, order, and public safety.

topics.title: Structure of Indian Judiciary: Integrated System
aliases: Supreme Court Chief Justice New Delhi
learning_objectives: Describe integrated judicial hierarchy in India: Supreme Court (apex at New Delhi), High Courts (state level), and District/Subordinate Courts.
Explain role of Lok Adalat for speedy dispute resolution.
topics.explanation:
India has a single integrated judicial system structured like a pyramid:
- Supreme Court: Apex court in New Delhi, headed by Chief Justice of India (CJI). Decisions binding on all Indian courts.
- High Courts: Highest judicial authority in states (e.g. Gujarat High Court at Ahmedabad).
- Subordinate/District Courts: District & Sessions courts at district level.
Lok Adalats (People's Courts) provide fast, inexpensive amicable settlements.
examples: Gujarat High Court is located at Sola in Ahmedabad.
Lok Adalats resolve long-pending motor accident claims and civil disputes through mutual compromise without court fees.
exercises: Describe the structure of the judicial system in India.
Is the decision of the Supreme Court of India binding on all lower courts in India?
What is the main objective of Lok Adalats?
solutions: It is an integrated pyramid system with the Supreme Court at the apex, High Courts at state level, and District/Subordinate Courts at district level.
Yes.
To provide speedy, informal, and inexpensive justice through mutual compromise without heavy litigation costs.
practice_questions: Where is the Supreme Court of India situated?
Whose decision is final and binding on all lower courts in India?

topics.title: Independence of Judiciary and Civil vs Criminal Cases
aliases: Criminal cases theft murder FIR police
learning_objectives: Explain Independence of Judiciary (free from executive and legislative interference).
Differentiate between Civil Law (property, rent, divorce) and Criminal Law (theft, assault, murder, FIR).
topics.explanation:
Independence of Judiciary ensures judges decide cases without political or executive pressure (protected tenure, fixed salaries from Consolidated Fund). Branches of Law:
- Civil Law: Deals with disputes over property, land purchase, contracts, rent, divorce. Remedy: Compensation or specific performance.
- Criminal Law: Deals with conduct considered offenses against society (theft, robbery, dowry harassment, murder). Begins with filing First Information Report (FIR) at police station.
examples: A dispute over property boundary between two neighbors is tried under Civil Law.
A case of armed robbery begins with an FIR filed at police station under Criminal Law.
exercises: Why is independence of the judiciary essential in a democracy?
Differentiate between Civil Law and Criminal Law with examples.
solutions: It ensures judges can deliver impartial justice without fear or pressure from politicians, officials, or powerful individuals.
Civil Law handles private disputes like land or contract disagreements; Criminal Law handles offenses against public order like theft or assault starting with an FIR.
practice_questions: What is an FIR?
Which branch of law applies to a tenant eviction dispute?
practice_solutions: First Information Report registered at a police station to report a cognizable crime.

topics.title: Public Interest Litigation (PIL) and Access to Justice
aliases: access to justice legal aid poor
learning_objectives: Explain Public Interest Litigation (PIL) introduced by Supreme Court in 1980s (Justice P.N. Bhagwati).
Analyze how PIL simplifies legal access for poor and marginalized citizens.
topics.explanation: In 1980s, Supreme Court devised Public Interest Litigation (PIL) so that any individual or organization can file a court petition on behalf of poor or disadvantaged citizens whose rights are violated. Even a postcard addressed to High Court or Supreme Court can be treated as a PIL petition. PILs led to landmark rulings on bonded labor, mid-day meals, and environmental protection.
examples: A PIL petition filed in Supreme Court led to mandatory provision of hot cooked Mid-Day Meals in all government primary schools.
Justice P.N. Bhagwati played a pioneering role in developing PIL jurisprudence in India.
exercises: What is a Public Interest Litigation (PIL)?
How has PIL made access to justice easier for poor and illiterate citizens?
solutions: A legal mechanism allowing any public-spirited person or group to file a court case on behalf of others whose rights have been infringed.
It simplified procedure so that even a letter or postcard describing rights violation can be treated as a writ petition without hiring expensive lawyers.
practice_questions: Name one Supreme Court judge associated with introducing PILs in India.
Give one example of a social cause addressed through a PIL.
practice_solutions: Justice P.N. Bhagwati (or Justice V.R. Krishna Iyer).
Enforcement of Mid-Day Meal Scheme in schools or release of bonded laborers.

topics.title: Understanding Social Justice and Marginalised Groups
learning_objectives: Define Social Justice (fair treatment, equal opportunity, and elimination of socio-economic discrimination).
Identify Marginalised groups: Scheduled Castes (SC), Scheduled Tribes (ST/Adivasis), and Other Backward Classes (OBC).
topics.explanation: Social Justice means creating an egalitarian society where every individual, regardless of caste, creed, gender, or tribe, enjoys equal rights, dignity, and economic opportunity. Marginalised groups (SC, ST Adivasis, OBCs) faced historical exclusion from land, education, and political power. Promoting social justice requires targeted affirmative policies.
examples: Adivasis (Scheduled Tribes) have deep cultural connections with forest land and minerals.
Reservation policy in educational institutions ensures seat quota for SC, ST, and OBC students.
exercises: What is meant by Social Justice?
Who are Adivasis?
solutions: The principle of ensuring equal rights, opportunities, and socio-economic dignity for all citizens without discrimination.
Indigenous tribal communities who have traditionally lived in close harmony with forests and nature.
practice_questions: Name three categories of marginalized communities recognized for affirmative protection in India.
Why do marginalized groups require constitutional safeguards?
practice_solutions: Scheduled Castes (SC), Scheduled Tribes (ST), and Other Backward Classes (OBC).
To overcome historical disadvantage, social discrimination, and economic inequality.

topics.title: Constitutional Provisions for Equality and Reservation
learning_objectives: Analyze Constitutional provisions: Article 15 (prohibits discrimination), Article 17 (abolishes Untouchability).
Explain Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act 1989.
topics.explanation:
Constitutional Guarantees:
- Article 15: Prohibits discrimination on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex, or place of birth.
- Article 17: Abolishes Untouchability and makes its practice a punishable crime.
- Reservation Policy: Provides quota in government jobs and educational admissions for SC, ST, and OBCs.
- Prevention of Atrocities Act (1989): Protects SC/ST individuals from physical assault, humiliation, or land grab.
examples: Article 17 makes practicing untouchability in any form an illegal punishable offense under Indian law.
Prevention of Atrocities Act 1989 penalizes anyone forcing SC/ST members to eat inedible substances or illegally occupying their land.
exercises: Which Article of the Indian Constitution abolishes the practice of Untouchability?
What is the main objective of the SC and ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act of 1989?
solutions: Article 17.
To protect Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes against violent atrocities, social humiliation, and land dispossession.
practice_questions: What does Article 15 of the Constitution mandate?
Why is reservation in public employment provided to SC and ST communities?
practice_solutions: It prohibits state discrimination against any citizen based on religion, race, caste, sex, or place of birth.
To ensure adequate representation of historically underrepresented communities in state administration.

topics.title: Social Anomalies: Child Labour, Gender Bias and Eradication Laws
learning_objectives: Examine social anomalies: Child Labour and Gender Discrimination.
Explain Child Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act and initiatives like Beti Bachao Beti Padhao.
topics.explanation:
Social anomalies are social evils retarding progress:
- Child Labour: Employing children under 14 in hazardous work violates Right to Education. Child Labour Act prohibits child employment in all occupations.
- Gender Discrimination: Bias against girl child leading to female foeticide and lower literacy. Initiatives like 'Beti Bachao Beti Padhao' promote girl education and health.
examples: Employing children under 14 in tea stalls, firework factories, or domestic work is illegal under Child Labour Act.
'Beti Bachao Beti Padhao' scheme aims to improve child sex ratio and promote higher education for girls.
exercises: What is the minimum age limit under Child Labour Prohibition laws below which employing children is illegal?
Name the national government initiative launched to prevent female foeticide and educate the girl child.
solutions: 14 years of age.
Beti Bachao, Beti Padhao.
practice_questions: How does child labour affect a child's fundamental right to education?
State two measures to eliminate gender bias in rural society.
practice_solutions: It deprives children of school attendance, physical health, and intellectual development.
Ensuring equal girl school enrollment and strictly enforcing laws against female foeticide and dowry.

learning_objectives: Identify essential Public Facilities (safe drinking water, sanitation, electricity, public transport, healthcare, primary education).

topics.explanation: Public facilities are essential basic needs required by every citizen (clean drinking water, public sanitation, electricity, primary health centers, government schools, public buses). Private companies operate for profit and would charge high rates affordable only to the rich. Therefore, government bears constitutional responsibility to ensure affordable universal access.
examples: Municipal Corporations supply chlorinated tap water at nominal subsidized rates to all city households.
Government Primary Health Centers (PHCs) provide free pulse polio vaccinations and maternal healthcare.

Why should the government, rather than private companies, be responsible for providing public facilities?

Private companies seek profit and charge high prices, whereas government ensures universal affordable access as a public duty regardless of income.

topics.title: Government Welfare Schemes and Economic Infrastructure

learning_objectives: Explain major social welfare schemes: Public Distribution System (PDS / Fair Price Shops), Mid-Day Meal (PM-POSHAN), MNREGA, and Ayushman Bharat.

topics.explanation:
Government runs Targeted Welfare Schemes:
- PDS (Public Distribution System): Provides subsidized food grains (wheat, rice) through Fair Price Shops to ration card holders.
- Mid-Day Meal Scheme: Provides free nutritious hot lunch to primary school students, improving attendance.
- MNREGA (2005): Guarantees 100 days of wage employment per year to rural households.
- Ayushman Bharat (PMJAY): Provides free health insurance coverage up to Rs 5 lakh per family.
examples: Fair Price Shops in Gujarat distribute subsidized wheat and rice to BPL (Below Poverty Line) card holders.
MNREGA provides 100 days guaranteed wage labor building check dams and rural roads.
exercises: What is the main objective of the Public Distribution System (PDS)?
How many days of guaranteed wage employment does MNREGA provide to rural households annually?

100 days per financial year.

topics.title: Consumer Awareness, Consumer Rights and Responsibilities
aliases: ISI AGMARK BIS hallmark standard marks
learning_objectives: Identify Consumer Rights (Right to Safety, Right to Information, Right to Choice, Right to Redressal) under Consumer Protection Act (COPRA 2019).
Recognize quality certification marks (ISI, AGMARK, BIS Hallmark) and consumer responsibilities (demanding cash memo/bill).
topics.explanation:
Consumers are often exploited through adulteration, false weight, or defective goods. Slogan 'Jago Grahak Jago' promotes consumer awareness. Consumer Protection Act (COPRA 2019) grants rights:
1) Right to Safety
2) Right to Information (expiry date, MRP)
3) Right to Choose
4) Right to Redressal (District, State, National Consumer Commissions).
Consumers must check quality standard marks (ISI for electricals, AGMARK for agricultural products, BIS Hallmark for gold) and insist on a Cash Memo/Bill.
examples: Checking ISI mark on electric irons and AGMARK seal on honey bottles ensures product safety and quality.
A consumer can file a complaint in District Consumer Forum if a shopkeeper sells an expired food product above MRP.
exercises: What slogan is used in national awareness campaigns to make consumers vigilant?
Name two quality standard marks consumers should check before buying electrical goods and food products.
solutions: 'Jago Grahak Jago'.
ISI mark for electrical goods and AGMARK for food/agricultural products.
practice_questions: Why should a consumer always demand a Cash Memo (bill) while buying goods?
Which certification mark guarantees the purity of gold jewelry?
